title: The stranger, the widow, the orphan (Exodus 22:21–27)
hookLine: you were strangers in Egypt; if he cries to me, I will hear

lines: YOUR FIRST WEEK IN A NEW COUNTRY.
THE WRONG LINE, THE WRONG FORM.
THE LAW TURNS TO THAT PERSON.
cards: It's your first week in a new country. You don't know which line to stand in. You can't read the forms.
Someone at a counter speaks to you slowly and loudly, as if you were a child, and the people behind you sigh. You smile, because you need what's at the end of that line.
A new school, a new job, a hospital in another city can give a small taste of it.
Right after the ten words, Exodus starts filling in what they look like on the ground, and soon the law turns to exactly that person: the one who doesn't belong yet.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew word for stranger is ger: someone living among a people who isn't one of them.
Not a tourist. A neighbor without roots, without land, without family to stand up for him. And notice the reason.
Not politeness. Memory. You were the ones in the wrong line once.

teach.h: YOU KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.
teach.b: A chapter later the law says it more tenderly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Then the circle widens. "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child."
In the world of the text, a widow or an orphan could easily be left with no one to speak for them, and nothing to stop them being pushed aside.

And here God steps in personally: if you afflict them and they cry to me, I will surely hear their cry. Then the law gets very small and practical. If you lend to a poor neighbor, don't charge interest.

teach.h: GIVE BACK THE CLOAK BY SUNDOWN.
teach.b: If you take his cloak as a pledge, give it back before the sun goes down, because "that is his covering only," and wherein shall he sleep?

teach.h: FOR YE WERE STRANGERS IN THE LAND OF EGYPT.
teach.b: God's reason: "when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious." Some Christians hear an echo in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus says, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in."
The stranger, the widow, the orphan: three people with no one else to stand up for them.

how: Some churches run food pantries, refugee resettlement programs and ministries to widows and orphans, and some Christians cite Exodus 22 and Matthew 25 together when explaining why.

o: ger: someone living among a people not their own
a traveler passing through for a night or two
an enemy soldier taken captive in a war

games.q: who the law protects — tap the pairs.
p: no one to speak for them in court
a cloak taken as a pledge
returned before the sun goes down

s: the reason given for welcoming strangers is good manners
the reason is memory: ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
the law says God himself will hear the widow's cry
"they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry."
the law lets a lender keep a poor man's cloak overnight
it goes back by sundown: it's his only covering. wherein shall he sleep?

games.q: you lent money to a poor neighbor and took his cloak as a pledge. the sun is setting, and he hasn't paid. what does the law say?
o: keep the cloak until he pays.
give it back before the sun goes down.
sell it to cover the debt.
games.why: give it back by sundown: "that is his covering only." the law cares where the poor man will sleep tonight.

practice: Remember a time you were the stranger, new, lost, unsure where to stand, and feel it again for a moment.

Then think of someone who's there now, a new coworker, a family who just moved in, someone grieving, and one small thing you could give: food, money, time, a name remembered. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: The stranger. In Hebrew, ger: someone living among you without land or family. The law protects him because Israel remembers being one.

orig.note: Hebrew: a stranger or resident foreigner, someone living among a people without land or kin there.

carryVoice: Your line: you were strangers too. Memory can make a heart kind. Day three hundred ninety-six, done.
